blocks.text: 1. Problem Statement
blocks.content: 1. Problem Statement

blocks.text:
Think about what actually happens the moment you type a message to a friend and hit send. The app does not dial a phone number and wait for someone to pick up. It does not poll a server every few seconds asking "anything new for me?" Instead, somewhere in the background, your phone has been holding a connection open to a server, quietly, for as long as the app has been running, and the instant you tap send, that message travels down a persistent pipe that was already there, waiting.

That is the problem this document is about: design a real-time messaging platform like WhatsApp, one that lets over a billion people exchange text, photos, videos, and voice notes instantly, in one-on-one chats and in groups of up to a few hundred people, whether the recipient's phone is sitting right there unlocked or asleep in someone's pocket on the other side of the world.

The naive version of this problem sounds almost like the URL shortener problem restated: accept a piece of data, store it, hand it to someone else later. But messaging breaks that comparison almost immediately, because a redirect service only ever has to answer "where does this short code point," a question with exactly one right answer that never changes. A messaging platform has to answer a much harder, constantly shifting question: "where is this specific human being, right now, at this exact millisecond, so I can hand them a message the instant it exists?" That single question, answered correctly at the scale of a billion concurrent users, is what makes this one of the hardest and most rewarding systems to design in an interview.

Six ideas make this system genuinely distinctive, and each one gets real depth in this document rather than a passing mention: a connection registry that maps every online user to the one specific server holding their live socket, delivery guarantees built around at-least-once semantics plus client-side deduplication, strict per-chat message ordering, the fan-out cost of a single message reaching two hundred people in a group at once, durable offline delivery backed by a push notification handoff, and end-to-end encryption deep enough to explain why the server routing your messages can never actually read them.

blocks.content: 2.1 The must-haves

["Send a one-on-one message: Alice writes something and Bob, whoever and wherever he is, eventually receives it, in the order Alice sent it relative to her other messages in that same chat.","Send a group message: the same guarantee, except now it has to reach every member of a group, which might be two people or two hundred.","Deliver messages while offline: if the recipient is not connected right now, the message must still be waiting for them the moment they reconnect, it cannot simply be dropped.","Show delivery state: the sender needs to know whether a message merely reached the server, actually reached the recipient's device, or was opened and read, the familiar single tick, double tick, and blue tick progression.","Send media: photos, videos, and voice notes need to travel through the system without treating a ten megabyte video the same way as a forty byte text message.","Presence: a chat should be able to show whether the other person is online right now or when they were last seen."]
items: Send a one-on-one message: Alice writes something and Bob, whoever and wherever he is, eventually receives it, in the order Alice sent it relative to her other messages in that same chat.
Send a group message: the same guarantee, except now it has to reach every member of a group, which might be two people or two hundred.
Deliver messages while offline: if the recipient is not connected right now, the message must still be waiting for them the moment they reconnect, it cannot simply be dropped.

Show delivery state: the sender needs to know whether a message merely reached the server, actually reached the recipient's device, or was opened and read, the familiar single tick, double tick, and blue tick progression.
Send media: photos, videos, and voice notes need to travel through the system without treating a ten megabyte video the same way as a forty byte text message.
Presence: a chat should be able to show whether the other person is online right now or when they were last seen.

blocks.content: 3.2 Availability

blocks.text: A messaging app that is down is not a minor inconvenience, it is a product people stop trusting within days. blocks.text: 3.3 Reliability
blocks.content: 3.3 Reliability

blocks.text: Once a message has been accepted by the server, it must not be lost, ever, even if the recipient does not come online again for a week. Losing a message here is not a performance hiccup, it is the digital equivalent of a letter vanishing in the mail, and it is exactly the kind of failure that erodes trust in a product permanently.

blocks.content: 3.4 Performance

blocks.content: 3.5 Fault Tolerance

blocks.text: Individual components will fail constantly at this scale, a gateway box will crash with thousands of live sockets on it, a database shard will get slow, a region will have a bad network day. The system has to keep functioning through all of that, degrading gracefully rather than taking the whole product down because one piece had a bad afternoon.

blocks.text: 3.6 Consistency
blocks.content: 3.6 Consistency

blocks.text: Consistency needs are not uniform across this system, and being honest about that is more valuable than pretending everything needs to be strongly consistent. A message must never be silently lost once accepted, that demands strong durability guarantees on the write path. Whether a friend's presence indicator says "online" a second later than reality is completely fine, that is a place eventual consistency is not just acceptable, it is the right engineering choice.

blocks.text: Start with the assumption from Section 5: 500 million daily active users, each sending about 40 messages a day. blocks.text: Here is the number that actually surprises people the first time they compute it. Of the 20 billion messages sent per day, 80% are 1:1, which is 16 billion messages, each needing exactly one delivery. The other 20%, 4 billion messages, go to groups with an average size of 50 members, and each of those needs to be delivered to roughly 49 other people. That is 4,000,000,000 * 49, which comes out to 196 billion delivery events from group messages alone. Add the 16 billion 1:1 deliveries and the system is handling roughly 212 billion delivery events a day, an average of about 2.45 million deliveries per second, with peak load landing north of 7 million deliveries per second. Group chats are one fifth of the messages sent and something like 92% of the actual delivery work. That single fact is the entire justification for why Section 8 gives fan-out its own dedicated component rather than folding it into the message service as an afterthought.

blocks.text: Not all 500 million daily users are connected at the same instant, people's phones sleep, apps get backgrounded, connections drop. A reasonable estimate is that around 15% of daily active users are concurrently connected at any given peak moment, which works out to 75 million simultaneous open WebSocket connections. Divide 75 million by 50,000 and the fleet needs to be roughly 1,500 gateway servers at peak, purely to hold sockets open, before a single message has even been routed.

blocks.text: 6.4 Storage over time
blocks.content: 6.4 Storage over time

blocks.text: Because messages are deleted from the server once every device confirms delivery, the message store is not growing forever, it is bounded by a rolling window of undelivered and recently delivered content, roughly 30 days of worst case buildup. Assume an average message record, ciphertext plus metadata, weighs in around 1 kilobyte. Thirty days of the full 20 billion messages a day comes to 20,000,000,000 * 30, which is 600 billion message rows in the absolute worst case where nothing ever gets cleaned up early, at roughly 1 kilobyte each that is around 600 terabytes. In practice the real working set is much smaller than that ceiling, because the overwhelming majority of messages are delivered and purged within seconds of being sent, not thirty days later, but sizing for the worst case is what keeps this design honest under load.

blocks.text: 6.6 Memory for the connection registry
blocks.content: 6.6 Memory for the connection registry

blocks.text: The connection registry, the structure mapping a userId to the specific gateway and socket holding their live connection, has to hold an entry for every one of those 75 million concurrent connections. Each entry is tiny, maybe 100 bytes: a userId, a gatewayId, a socket identifier, a last heartbeat timestamp. Seventy five million times 100 bytes is about 7.5 gigabytes, trivially small, comfortably fitting in memory across a small sharded Redis cluster with enormous headroom to spare.

blocks.text: Any estimate worth presenting has to survive being wrong. If real peak delivery load came in ten times higher than this section projects, somewhere past 70 million deliveries a second, does the design still hold together? Yes, because every layer in this system, the gateway tier, the fan-out worker pool, the message store shards, was built to scale horizontally from the start. Ten times the load means roughly ten times the machines at each of those layers, not a redesign. The one place that genuinely needs forethought rather than just more hardware is the connection registry, since it has to stay fast and available even as the number of entries it tracks grows by an order of magnitude, which is exactly why Section 18 spends real time on how that store itself gets sharded and replicated.

blocks.text: Alice sends a message over her already-open WebSocket connection to Gateway A. blocks.text: 7.4 Why a gateway cannot just be a load-balanced REST server
blocks.content: 7.4 Why a gateway cannot just be a load-balanced REST server

blocks.text: It is worth being explicit about why this tier looks so different from a typical stateless API fleet. A REST server holds no state between one request and the next, any instance can answer any request, and a load balancer is free to send consecutive requests from the same client to entirely different machines without anyone noticing. A connection gateway is the opposite: the moment a client's WebSocket handshake completes on Gateway A, that specific TCP connection lives on Gateway A and nowhere else, for as long as the app stays connected, sometimes for hours. That single fact, that state now lives pinned to one specific machine instead of floating freely across the fleet, is the root cause behind the sticky-session load balancing story in Section 16 and the careful, connection-draining deploy story in Section 27. Nearly every unusual constraint in this design traces back to this one architectural fact.

blocks.text: 11.1 SQL versus NoSQL, entity by entity
blocks.content: 11.1 SQL versus NoSQL, entity by entity

blocks.text: Not every entity in this system wants the same kind of database, and pretending otherwise usually produces a worse design than picking honestly per entity. The messages table is by far the highest write volume, append-mostly, and almost always queried by a single chatId, which is exactly the access pattern a wide-column store like Cassandra or ScyllaDB was built for, so that is what it runs on. Users, devices, and chat metadata are comparatively low volume, need relational integrity, joins, and transactions when a group's membership changes, so a conventional relational database is the better fit there. Presence, covered already in Section 8.2, is not really a database at all in the traditional sense, it is a fast, ephemeral, in-memory store like Redis, because it does not need durability beyond a short TTL, it needs raw speed.

blocks.content: 11.3 What sharding by chat_id costs us

blocks.text: No sharding key is free, and this one has a real cost worth naming honestly: a single user's total message history is now scattered across as many shards as they have distinct chats, which would make a query like "show me everything Alice has ever sent, across every conversation" expensive. Her phone generates a clientMessageId, encrypts the text using the session key already established with Bob's device, and sends a SEND_MESSAGE frame over her open connection to Gateway A. blocks.text: Only after that does the message service ask the presence service where Bob is, and the answer comes back offline, no gateway currently holds his connection. Minutes later, Bob's phone buzzes, the OS wakes the app in the background, and it reconnects, this time landing on Gateway A again purely by chance of load balancing. The moment that connection registers, the message service drains Bob's offline queue, finds the pending message, and delivers it down his freshly opened socket. Bob's client sends back an ACK_DELIVERED, the message service updates the stored state to DELIVERED, and Alice's client flips to a double grey tick. A little later, Bob actually opens the chat and reads it, his client fires an ACK_READ, the state moves to READ, and Alice sees the familiar double blue tick, the entire loop closed without either person ever having to refresh or retry anything manually.

blocks.text: Now consider the failure case that at-least-once delivery exists to handle. Alice sends message m7, the message service persists it and sends back a SENT acknowledgment, but her phone loses signal for a moment and never receives it. From her client's point of view, it genuinely does not know whether m7 made it or not, so after a short timeout, it does the only safe thing: it retries, resending the exact same frame with the exact same clientMessageId. blocks.content: 13.3 The receipt state machine

blocks.alt: A message moves through exactly three states in order, SENT, then DELIVERED, then READ, and the ticks on screen are a direct reflection of that state

blocks.text: It is worth stating the state machine explicitly, because the familiar tick marks are not a UI flourish, they are a literal rendering of server-tracked state. SENT means the server has durably accepted the message, a single grey tick. DELIVERED means at least one of the recipient's devices has actually received it over a live connection, a double grey tick. READ means the recipient opened the chat and their client explicitly acknowledged it, a double blue tick. Transitions only ever move forward, never backward, and for a group chat, the client typically shows the most conservative state, delivered only once every member has received it, read only once every member has read it, though some products relax that and show per-member detail instead.

blocks.text: The recent-messages cache is append-only in the common case, a new message in a chat gets pushed onto the cached list and the oldest entry gets trimmed off, a simple fixed-length structure that never needs a complicated invalidation strategy. blocks.alt: A failed delivery job retries with exponential backoff a handful of times before landing in a dead letter queue for manual or automated inspection

blocks.text: A delivery job can fail for reasons that have nothing to do with the message itself, a downstream push provider having a bad minute, a transient network blip to a specific gateway. Every consumer retries a failed job a bounded number of times, typically five, with exponential backoff between attempts so a struggling downstream dependency does not get hammered harder by the retries meant to help it recover. A job that still fails after those attempts, commonly caused by something genuinely wrong like an expired device push token, lands in a dead letter queue rather than being silently dropped or retried forever, where it can be inspected, and in the push token case, trigger a cleanup of that stale registration.

blocks.text: 16.1 Why WebSocket load balancing is not like REST load balancing
blocks.content: 16.1 Why WebSocket load balancing is not like REST load balancing
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-problem-images/1785229089021-802071532.png
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-problem-images/1785229089021-802071532.png
blocks.alt: A WebSocket connection gets balanced exactly once, at handshake time, then stays pinned to that one gateway for its entire lifetime

blocks.text: A REST load balancer makes a fresh decision on every single request, and it is free to send two consecutive requests from the same client to two entirely different backend instances without anyone ever noticing. A connection gateway breaks that assumption completely: once a client's WebSocket handshake lands on Gateway A, every single frame for that connection, for the entire life of that session, has to go to Gateway A, because that is physically where the socket lives. There is no way to transparently hand a live TCP connection off to a different machine mid-flight. That is what people mean by a sticky session, and it is not a preference here, it is a hard constraint imposed by how TCP and WebSockets work.

blocks.text: 16.2 Two tiers: connect-time and always-on
blocks.content: 16.2 Two tiers: connect-time and always-on

blocks.text: The load balancing story here actually has two distinct layers doing two different jobs. At connect time, a standard layer 4 or layer 7 load balancer picks which gateway a new WebSocket handshake lands on, typically using something close to round robin or least-connections, and that decision matters a lot because it is the only chance the system ever gets to balance that particular connection's load. After that single decision, the load balancer is essentially out of the picture for that connection's entire lifetime, all subsequent traffic for it flows directly, or through a lightweight pass-through, straight to the gateway that accepted the handshake. This is fundamentally different from the REST path, where the load balancer touches every single request, not just the first one.

https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-problem-images/1785396013271-259607789.png
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-problem-images/1785396013271-259607789.png
blocks.alt: Every socket on a crashed gateway drops at once, and a jittered reconnect spreads those clients back across the healthy fleet instead of overwhelming it

blocks.text: This is one of the most instructive failure scenarios in the entire system, worth walking through in an interview even if nobody asks directly. Gateway 14 crashes, and every one of the roughly 50,000 sockets it was holding drops simultaneously. Each of those clients detects the disconnect and attempts to reconnect, but if all 50,000 retried at the exact same instant, they would slam the load balancer and whichever gateways happen to catch them with a sudden, correlated spike, a self-inflicted denial of service. The fix is jittered exponential backoff, each client waits a randomized amount of time before its first retry, spreading 50,000 simultaneous reconnect attempts into a smoothed-out wave over a few seconds instead of a single spike. Meanwhile, presence entries for those users go stale until either a heartbeat TTL expires or the new connection simply overwrites the old mapping, and any message routed to them in that window safely falls into the offline queue path rather than being lost, exactly the graceful degradation Section 3.5 asked for.

blocks.content: 21.2 End to end encryption, in depth
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-problem-images/1785229102103-868309116.png
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-problem-images/1785229102103-868309116.png
blocks.alt: An initial key agreement establishes a shared root key, and every subsequent message ratchets that key forward into a fresh, single-use key

blocks.text: This is the section that most separates a serious messaging design from a toy one, so it is worth genuine depth. Two devices that have never talked before first perform a key agreement, conceptually similar to the Signal protocol's X3DH, Extended Triple Diffie-Hellman, exchange, producing a shared secret neither the server nor anyone eavesdropping on the wire could derive on their own. From that shared secret, both sides derive a starting root key, and this is where the double ratchet idea comes in: every single message that follows advances the key material forward, deriving a fresh, single-use symmetric key for that one message alone, and periodically performing a new Diffie-Hellman step that ratchets the root key itself forward too. The payoff is two distinct and valuable properties. Forward secrecy means that if an attacker somehow compromises a device's current key material, they gain nothing about messages sent before that point, since those messages were encrypted with keys that no longer exist anywhere. Post-compromise security means the reverse, once the ratchet advances again after a compromise, future messages are protected again too, even without the user doing anything special. Group chats extend this with something called Sender Keys, where each member establishes one key that every other member can use to decrypt that sender's messages, so encrypting a group message costs roughly one encryption operation regardless of group size, rather than one separate pairwise encryption per recipient, which is what would happen if a group of 200 tried to reuse the pairwise ratchet directly.

blocks.text: 21.3 What the server can and cannot do because of this
blocks.content: 21.3 What the server can and cannot do because of this

blocks.text: The server routes ciphertext it has no ability to read, full stop, and that single fact has real, unavoidable product consequences worth stating plainly rather than glossing over. Server-side search across message content is simply impossible, if search is a feature at all, it has to run entirely on-device, over content the client has already decrypted locally, with any index it builds staying local too. Automated content moderation of message bodies is equally impossible, which is exactly why real encrypted messaging platforms lean on metadata signals instead, sending rate, group report volume, spam-pattern detection on unencrypted routing information, rather than content scanning. Rich link previews for a shared URL have to be generated client-side too, since the server never sees the URL to fetch a preview for it itself. None of this is a gap in the design, it is the direct and honest trade-off of choosing real end-to-end encryption, and being able to explain it clearly is exactly the kind of depth that separates a strong system design answer from a shallow one.

blocks.text: 23.1 The presence service
blocks.content: 23.1 The presence service

blocks.text: Every single routing decision in the system depends on a presence lookup, which makes it, if built naively as one unsharded instance, the most dangerous single point of failure in the whole design. The mitigation is twofold: run it as a sharded, replicated in-memory cluster rather than a single box, and, just as importantly, design every caller to treat a presence lookup failure or timeout as "assume offline" rather than an error that blocks the send. That second choice means a presence outage degrades the system to slightly slower, queue-based delivery for everyone, never a total failure.

blocks.text: Bob rides the subway, his phone loses and regains signal every thirty seconds as the train passes through tunnels. Naively marking him offline the instant his socket drops, and online again the instant he reconnects, would fire a storm of presence updates and, worse, could trigger a redundant push notification for a message that would have been delivered live within seconds anyway. A short grace period before a connection drop is treated as a real "offline" transition absorbs this kind of flapping cleanly, and reconnect attempts themselves use the same jittered backoff described in Section 20.1 so a train full of phones losing signal at once does not create its own miniature reconnect storm.

blocks.text: A fan-out job for a 200 member group delivers to 100 members successfully before the worker processing it crashes. Because the job itself, not just the underlying message, is tracked durably in the fan-out queue rather than only living in a worker's in-memory state, a replacement worker picks up the same job and resumes, and because delivery to an individual recipient is itself idempotent, the fact that some of the first 100 might be retried causes no harm, they simply receive a delivery attempt for a message they may have already gotten, deduplicated the same way described in Section 13.2.

"How does multi-device work without breaking end-to-end encryption?" Each device has its own identity key and its own ratchet session with every contact, so a message gets encrypted once per recipient device rather than once per recipient account.

"How would you detect spam without reading message content?" Behavioral and metadata signals, sending rate anomalies, a burst of new-chat creation, high report volume from recipients, never content inspection.

"What changes for a channel with a hundred thousand subscribers instead of a two hundred person group?" Fan-out at that scale usually shifts from a push-to-everyone model toward a pull or CDN-backed broadcast model, since actively pushing to a hundred thousand sockets for one post stops being the right lever.

"How do you handle a user blocking another user?" A check in the message service's authorization step, alongside the chat-membership check from Section 21.1, silently drops or rejects messages from a blocked sender before they are ever persisted.

import time
from dataclasses import dataclass
from threading import Lock
from typing import Optional


@dataclass
class Connection:
    # A tiny immutable record of exactly where one user's live socket lives.
    gateway_id: str
    socket_id: str
    last_heartbeat_millis: int


class ConnectionRegistry:
    def __init__(self):
        # In production this is a sharded, replicated Redis cluster, not a
        # single process's memory, but the semantics it exposes are the same.
        self._user_to_connection = {}
        self._lock = Lock()

    def register(self, user_id, gateway_id, socket_id):
        with self._lock:
            self._user_to_connection[user_id] = Connection(gateway_id, socket_id, int(time.time() * 1000))

    def heartbeat(self, user_id):
        with self._lock:
            existing = self._user_to_connection.get(user_id)
            if existing is not None:
                self._user_to_connection[user_id] = Connection(
                    existing.gateway_id, existing.socket_id, int(time.time() * 1000)
                )

    def deregister(self, user_id):
        with self._lock:
            self._user_to_connection.pop(user_id, None)

    def lookup(self, user_id, stale_after_millis) -> Optional[Connection]:
        # A user only counts as online if a heartbeat has been seen recently,
        # which is what lets a crashed gateway's stale entries self-expire.
        with self._lock:
            connection = self._user_to_connection.get(user_id)
            if connection is None:
                return None
            is_stale = int(time.time() * 1000) - connection.last_heartbeat_millis > stale_after_millis
            return None if is_stale else connection


if __name__ == "__main__":
    registry = ConnectionRegistry()
    registry.register("bob_42", "gateway-A", "socket-8842")

    found = registry.lookup("bob_42", 30_000)
    print(f"Bob is on: {found.gateway_id if found else 'offline'}")

    unknown = registry.lookup("carol_7", 30_000)
    print(f"Carol is on: {unknown.gateway_id if unknown else 'offline'}")

class PresenceService:
    STALE_AFTER_MILLIS = 30_000

    def __init__(self, connection_registry):
        self._connection_registry = connection_registry

    def is_online(self, user_id) -> bool:
        return self._connection_registry.lookup(user_id, self.STALE_AFTER_MILLIS) is not None

    def gateway_for(self, user_id):
        # Returns the specific gateway holding this user's connection, or None
        # if they are offline, which callers treat as "route to the offline path".
        connection = self._connection_registry.lookup(user_id, self.STALE_AFTER_MILLIS)
        return connection.gateway_id if connection else None


if __name__ == "__main__":
    from connection_registry import ConnectionRegistry  # co-located module in a real service

    registry = ConnectionRegistry()
    registry.register("bob_42", "gateway-A", "socket-8842")
    presence_service = PresenceService(registry)

    print(f"Bob online: {presence_service.is_online('bob_42')}")
    print(f"Bob's gateway: {presence_service.gateway_for('bob_42') or 'none'}")
    print(f"Carol online: {presence_service.is_online('carol_7')}")

from collections import defaultdict
from dataclasses import dataclass
from threading import Lock


@dataclass
class QueuedMessage:
    message_id: str
    chat_id: str
    ciphertext: str


class OfflineMessageQueue:
    def __init__(self):
        # In production this is a durable, per-user partition in a wide-column
        # store, not an in-memory dict, but the enqueue/drain contract is the same.
        self._queues_by_user = defaultdict(list)
        self._lock = Lock()

    def enqueue(self, user_id, message: QueuedMessage):
        with self._lock:
            self._queues_by_user[user_id].append(message)

    def drain(self, user_id):
        # Drains and clears the queue atomically, so a message is never handed
        # out twice even if drain is called again before delivery finishes.
        with self._lock:
            pending = self._queues_by_user.pop(user_id, [])
            return pending


if __name__ == "__main__":
    queue = OfflineMessageQueue()
    queue.enqueue("bob_42", QueuedMessage("m1", "chat_alice_bob", "<ciphertext>"))
    queue.enqueue("bob_42", QueuedMessage("m2", "chat_alice_bob", "<ciphertext>"))

    drained = queue.drain("bob_42")
    print(f"Delivered on reconnect: {len(drained)} messages")

    drained_again = queue.drain("bob_42")
    print(f"Second drain finds: {len(drained_again)} messages")

from dataclasses import dataclass
from enum import Enum
from threading import Lock
from typing import Dict


class State(Enum):
    SENT = "SENT"
    DELIVERED = "DELIVERED"
    READ = "READ"


@dataclass
class Message:
    message_id: str
    chat_id: str
    sender_id: str
    recipient_id: str
    ciphertext: str
    state: State = State.SENT


class MessageDeliveryService:
    def __init__(self, presence_service, offline_queue):
        self._presence_service = presence_service
        self._offline_queue = offline_queue
        # Dedup index: client_message_id -> message_id already persisted for it.
        # This is what makes retrying a send safe, exactly as walked through
        # in Section 13.2.
        self._seen_client_message_ids: Dict[str, str] = {}
        self._message_store: Dict[str, Message] = {}
        self._next_message_id = 1
        self._lock = Lock()

    def send(self, client_message_id, chat_id, sender_id, recipient_id, ciphertext) -> Message:
        # Safe to call twice with the same client_message_id, the second
        # call returns the original without creating a duplicate or
        # re-triggering delivery side effects.
        with self._lock:
            existing_message_id = self._seen_client_message_ids.get(client_message_id)
            if existing_message_id is not None:
                return self._message_store[existing_message_id]

            message_id = f"m{self._next_message_id}"
            self._next_message_id += 1
            message = Message(message_id, chat_id, sender_id, recipient_id, ciphertext)
            self._message_store[message_id] = message
            self._seen_client_message_ids[client_message_id] = message_id

        self._route(message, recipient_id)
        return message

    def _route(self, message: Message, recipient_id):
        gateway_id = self._presence_service.gateway_for(recipient_id)
        if gateway_id is not None:
            self._deliver_live(message, gateway_id)
        else:
            from offline_message_queue import QueuedMessage  # co-located module in a real service
            self._offline_queue.enqueue(
                recipient_id, QueuedMessage(message.message_id, message.chat_id, message.ciphertext)
            )
            self._trigger_push_notification(recipient_id)

    def _deliver_live(self, message: Message, gateway_id):
        # In production this hops to the recipient's specific gateway over
        # an internal RPC, exactly as shown in the gateway message hop diagram.
        print(f"Delivering {message.message_id} live via {gateway_id}")
        message.state = State.DELIVERED

    def _trigger_push_notification(self, recipient_id):
        print(f"Recipient {recipient_id} offline, push notification queued")

    def mark_delivered(self, message_id):
        message = self._message_store.get(message_id)
        if message:
            message.state = State.DELIVERED

    def mark_read(self, message_id):
        message = self._message_store.get(message_id)
        if message:
            message.state = State.READ


if __name__ == "__main__":
    from connection_registry import ConnectionRegistry
    from presence_service import PresenceService
    from offline_message_queue import OfflineMessageQueue

    registry = ConnectionRegistry()
    presence_service = PresenceService(registry)
    offline_queue = OfflineMessageQueue()
    delivery_service = MessageDeliveryService(presence_service, offline_queue)

    # Bob is offline: falls back to the offline queue plus a push notification.
    m1 = delivery_service.send("client-uuid-1", "chat_alice_bob", "alice_1", "bob_42", "<ciphertext>")
    print(f"First send state: {m1.state}")

    # Alice's client retries the exact same send after a lost ack.
    m1_retry = delivery_service.send("client-uuid-1", "chat_alice_bob", "alice_1", "bob_42", "<ciphertext>")
    print(f"Retry returns same message_id: {m1.message_id == m1_retry.message_id}")

    # Bob reconnects, presence gets registered, a new send now delivers live.
    registry.register("bob_42", "gateway-A", "socket-8842")
    m2 = delivery_service.send("client-uuid-2", "chat_alice_bob", "alice_1", "bob_42", "<ciphertext>")
    print(f"Second send state: {m2.state}")
